quick.summary: Why doing fewer things gives your team a real chance to succeed.
quick.takeaway: Pick one big win for the week, and protect it from extra noise.

parts.title: Packing the big win

beats.line: We promised thirty things this week. We finished ten, and everyone feels terrible. Why?
Imagine packing for a trip. You cannot shove your whole closet into one bag.
Right, I just pack what I need for the beach.
Your week is the same. Pack one clear outcome, not thirty random tasks.
This is known as a sprint goal commitment.
Can I just say the one big win?
Yes. The one big win. It gives the team focus.
So we pick the main thing and let the extra stuff wait?
But what if someone asks for a tiny new thing on Wednesday?

parts.cliff: How to say no on a Wednesday.

beats.line: Think of a train driving to a station.
If you stop for everyone waving on the road, you never arrive.
So that tiny Wednesday request is someone waving at the train?
Yes. Every tiny request adds up. You have to guard the schedule.
Put the new request on the list for next time.
I just tell them we are driving to the station right now?
Tell them it goes in the next bag you pack.
The team focuses on the big win, and I block the noise.
That is how you protect their time.

quiz.question: What should you do when a small new request arrives mid-week?
options: Save it for the next time you plan.
Stop the train to help immediately.
Add it to the current list.
Ask the team to work late.
quiz.explanation: Adding requests in the middle of the week derails the main goal.

quiz.question: Having thirty goals means your team will accomplish more this week.
quiz.explanation: Trying to do everything at once usually means nothing gets finished.
